objectives: Clarify a long word by splitting it into parts.
Find facts and numbers in a news report without falling for the number trap.
Ask your own Work it out question.
Use 3 new words: admitted, structural, opposite.

learn.title: Brief: Clarify with word parts
learn.body:
Today's toolkit focus: 🧐 **Clarify.** When you meet a long word, don't skip it. Split it into parts you know. "Structural" = **structure** + **-al** (about). So structural means "about how something is built". 🔧

Today's text is a **news report**. News reports are packed with facts: names, numbers, places. They also use **quotes** (words people really said), and quotes often hide a feeling or an opinion.

⚠️ **Number trap:** a report can have lots of numbers. Before you answer, check you've got the number for the right thing.

learn.title: 📚 Power words for today
items: **admitted** (verb): said that something is true, usually when it's a bit embarrassing. Use it: "He admitted he had forgotten his homework."

**structural** (adjective): about how something is built and holds together. structure + **-al**. A structural engineer makes sure bridges and buildings stay up. Use it: "The storm caused structural damage to the roof."
**opposite** (noun or adjective): completely different; the other way round. Use it: "My sister loves maths, but I'm the opposite."

learn.title: The report: Student engineers win with a bridge made of pasta
learn.body:
A team of four Grade 8 students has won the regional Young Engineers Challenge with a bridge made from nothing but dry spaghetti and glue.

The bridge weighed just 180 grams, yet it held 23 kilograms of sand before it finally cracked on Saturday afternoon. That is more than 120 times its own weight. The second-placed team's bridge, which was almost twice as heavy, gave way at 15 kilograms.

Team captain Lina Haddad, 13, said the group tested more than thirty small models in her family's kitchen before choosing their final design. "Most of them snapped in the first ten seconds," she admitted. "My dad stopped asking what was for dinner."

The winning bridge used triangles along both sides. Engineers love triangles because a triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides breaks or bends, while a square can easily be pushed sideways into a diamond shape.

Judge Omar Farouk, a structural engineer, said the result surprised him. "Every year, teams try to win by making their bridges thicker and heavier. This team did the opposite. They spent their time thinking instead of gluing."

The students will receive new laboratory equipment for their school and a visit to a construction site in the spring. When asked what she would like to build next, Lina did not hesitate. "Something people can actually walk across," she said.

learn.title: 🎧 Watch me think: an expert reader's thoughts
learn.body:
🔮 **Predict:** "A news report about a competition. I expect names, numbers and quotes."
🧐 **Clarify:** "'Regional'? Region + -al: about a region, an area. So it's a competition for this area, not the whole world."
🙋 **Question:** "How can a lighter bridge beat a heavier one? That's the big question."
🧠 **Infer:** "'My dad stopped asking what was for dinner.' Clue: thirty models in the kitchen. Think: it's a joke. Cooking had stopped."
📝 **Summarise:** "Students won because their clever, light design was stronger than heavier bridges."

Notice how the expert stopped at a word, split it, and kept going. Your turn now.

check.prompt: 🔮 Predict: Today's text is a news report called "Student engineers win with a bridge made of pasta". What will it most likely contain?
check.hint: Think about the type of text (a news report) and the headline. What do news reports usually give you?
options: Facts about a competition: who won, how they did it, and numbers about the bridge
A made-up story about a talking bridge
A recipe for spaghetti
A diary about a holiday
check.explanation: News reports give facts: who, what, where, when, how. The headline tells you it's about winning a competition. After reading, check: was your prediction right? Good readers change their prediction as they go.

check.prompt: 🔤 Word detective: "When asked what she would like to build next, Lina did not hesitate." What does "hesitate" mean here?
check.hint: If you "did not hesitate", did you answer fast or slowly? So what does hesitate mean?
options: Stop and wait for a moment because you're unsure
Laugh loudly
Build something quickly
Forget the question
check.explanation: To hesitate is to pause because you're unsure. "Did not hesitate" means she answered straight away: she already knew what she wanted to build.

check.prompt: 🔎 Find it: How much sand did the winning bridge hold before it cracked?
check.hint: Find the sentence about sand. Check the number belongs to the WINNING bridge.
options: 180 grams
15 kilograms
23 kilograms
120 kilograms
check.explanation: 23 kilograms. 180 grams is the bridge's own weight, 15 kilograms is the other team's result, and 120 is how many times its own weight. That's the number trap: every option is a number from the report.

check.prompt: 🧠 Work it out: Lina says, "My dad stopped asking what was for dinner." What does this suggest?
check.hint: Clue: where did the team test their models? Think about what that kitchen looked like for weeks.
options: The kitchen was so busy with bridge testing that normal dinners stopped happening
Her dad doesn't like spaghetti
Her dad was one of the judges
The family always eats at a restaurant
check.explanation: It's a joke. Clue: they tested more than thirty models in the kitchen. Think: a kitchen full of spaghetti and glue is not a place for cooking dinner, so her dad gave up asking.

check.prompt: 🧩 Clue hunt: The judge thinks the team won because they planned cleverly. Which sentence is the best proof?
check.hint: Look for the judge's own words about HOW the team worked.
options: "They spent their time thinking instead of gluing."
"The bridge weighed just 180 grams."
"Judge Omar Farouk, a structural engineer, said the result surprised him."
"The students will receive new laboratory equipment for their school."
check.explanation: "Thinking instead of gluing" is the judge saying their planning won it. The other sentences are true, but they don't prove anything about planning.

check.prompt: ✍️ Why did the writer...? Why does the writer explain why engineers use triangles?
check.hint: Read the paragraph just before the one about triangles. What would a reader want explained at that point?
options: To help readers understand why the bridge was so strong
To teach readers how to draw triangles
To show that squares are better
To turn the report into maths homework
check.explanation: The paragraph comes right after we hear how much weight the bridge held. It explains the secret behind that strength, so the reader understands the win.

check.prompt: 📝 Sum it up: In ONE sentence, what is this text mainly about? Start with: "This text is mainly about..."

markPoints.point: Says it's about students winning a competition with their spaghetti bridge

check.modelAnswer: This text is mainly about students who won a competition with a light spaghetti bridge that was stronger because of its clever design.
check.explanation: A good summary names WHO or WHAT the text is about and the MAIN thing that happens, in one sentence. Small details (numbers, colours, names of places) usually stay out.

check.prompt: 🙋 Your question: Write one Work it out question about the text: a question whose answer is NOT written in it.

markPoints.point: Asks a question that has to be worked out, not found (often starts with Why, How or What do you think)

check.modelAnswer: Why do you think the other teams kept making their bridges heavier?
check.explanation: Asking your own questions is one of the strongest reading habits there is. A Find it question ("What colour was the car?") is too easy. A Work it out question makes you think: "Why...?", "How did he feel when...?", "What do you think...?"

practice.prompt: 🗂️ Sort it: Is each question about today's text Find it, Work it out, or Why did the writer...?
practice.hint: Ask yourself: could I point at the answer with my finger? If not, is it about the text, or about the writer's choices?

rows.statement: How many students were in the team?
Why do you think the judge was surprised?
rows.explanation: Not written. Clue: other teams make bridges thicker and heavier.
It's written: lab equipment and a site visit.

rows.statement: Is Lina likely to keep building things? Why?
rows.explanation: Not written. Clue: she didn't hesitate about what to build next.

rows.statement: Why does the writer end the report with Lina's quote?
rows.explanation: It's about the effect: it ends on a funny, hopeful note.

rows.statement: Why does the writer say the bridge held more than 120 times its own weight?
rows.explanation: It's about the effect: it makes the result sound amazing.

practice.explanation: Find it = the answer is written in the text. Work it out = clue + think. Why did the writer = what a word or idea does to the reader.

practice.prompt: 💬 Own words: The second team's bridge was almost twice as heavy but held less. What does this tell you about building a strong bridge? Start with "This suggests that..." and use "because" to add your clue.

markPoints.point: Heavier / thicker is not always stronger; the shape or design matters more
Evidence: triangles / 23 kg against 15 kg / the judge's quote about thicker and heavier

practice.modelAnswer: This suggests that a heavier bridge is not always stronger and the design matters more, because the winning bridge used triangles and held 23 kilograms, while the heavier one broke at 15.
practice.explanation: One mark for the idea (shape and design beat weight). One mark for proof from the report (triangles, 23 kg against 15 kg, or the judge's words).

summary: Clarify long words by splitting them: structure + -al = structural.
News reports: facts for Find it, quotes for Work it out.
Number trap: check the number belongs to the right thing.
👪 Talk card for a parent (2 minutes): "What's the cleverest thing you've ever built or fixed?" and "Why did the lighter bridge win?"

flashcards.back: Split a long word into parts you know: structure + -al = about how something is built.
said something true that is a bit embarrassing
about how something is built and holds together
completely different; the other way round
